title: How New York Got Rich (It wasn’t Wall Street)
fullText: In 1821, New York exported $13 million of goods. That same year, Boston exported 12. Two ports, same ocean, same country, near enough level. 40 years later, in 1860, New York was exporting $145 million. Boston was on 17. Boston had not shrunk. It grew the way a successful city grows. New York grew more than 10 times over. It pulled away from every port on the continent and never came back to the pack. Something happened to one of those cities and not the other. The answer people reach for is Wall Street. That is backwards. Wall Street is what the machine produced. It is not the machine. What New York actually did was make four decisions in the space of about 8 years. a law about auctions, a shipping timetable, a ditch, and a detour through the American South. Every one of them is boring on its own. Together, they are the reason one island took the trade of a continent and never gave it back. Three of the four are almost never mentioned. The one everybody has heard of, the ditch, turns out not to be the biggest of them. Quick one for you before the first decision. A lot of you know the city better than any book I read for it. If you live in New York or you have spent a week there, name one thing, the thing about that place that nobody warned you about, not the famous thing, the thing you only find out by standing in it, and a second one for later. Some of you live in a town that the ditch built. I will name them in a couple minutes. When I do, tell me what is left of it where you are. Both in the comments. Leave a like on the way past and get yourself subscribed. The town's half of this is a video of its own. Start with what New York had before it decided anything. It has a genuinely superb harbor. That is not a small thing. It is not the answer either. So, it is worth being precise about what makes it good. The sea approach is short, about 17 mi. The upper bay is sheltered. The East River gives anchorage. Long Island Sound offers a protected back route. And the Hudson runs straight inland from it. It is also deep and it does not freeze. Depth sounds like a technicality. It stopped being one. Ships got bigger through the 1800s and Philadelphia sat up a shallow river. Ships that could dock in New York could not reach it. So, New York started with an advantage. It was not a secret and it was not enough. Boston had a harbor. So did Baltimore, Charleston, New Orleans, and Philadelphia. Every one of them had water, ships, merchants, and warehouses. A harbor is a door. Nobody had answered the question of what was on the other side of it. The historian who spent his career on this port, Robert Albian, was blunt about it. The geography was necessary. It explains nothing on its own. What mattered was what a small number of merchants did with it. So here is what they did. The first decision is about a glut. The war of 1812 ends. British factories have spent years unable to sell into America and they are sitting on mountains of unsold cloth. They want it gone. Not sold well. Gone. In 1817, New York State passes an act to regulate sales by public auction. It sounds like paperwork. It is a trap, and it is a good one. The law licenses auctioners and bonds them. It forces sales into designated auction rooms instead of the street or the pier, and it puts a tax on dutable goods sold at auction. What that gives a British manufacturer is certainty. Send a shipload to New York and it will sell. It might sell badly, but it will sell on a known day in a known room to real bidders. The auctioners went further and lent against the cargo. Houses like Hagerty and Austin would advance a foreign merchant what he needed before the sale. So a factory in Manchester could turn a warehouse of unsold cloth into cash fast without knowing a single American shopkeeper. Nowhere else offered that. So the cloth came to New York. The concentration this produced is hard to believe. By 1833, New York auctions were handling roughly 97% of all dutable auction sales in the United States. 97%. Not a lead, a monopoly in everything but name. Auction sales that year came to 13.16 million. 12.12 million of that was dutable goods. And now the part that makes this a machine rather than a lucky law. That tax on dutable goods sold at auction went to the cano fund. British manufacturers dumping surplus cloth in New York were helping to pay for the ditch. the ditch that would open the American interior to the same city. Nobody asked them to. One decision funding the next one. That is the shape of this whole story. The second decision is a timetable. Before 1818, a ship crossed the Atlantic when it was full. That was the rule everywhere. A merchant with cargo waited on the quay until the captain decided he had enough. You could not plan around it. You could not promise a customer a date. You could not tell a bank when your money would arrive. In 1817, a group of New York merchants set up what became the Black Ball line. On the 5th of January 1818, the James Monroe left New York for Liverpool on schedule. Four ships, fixed departure dates, sailing whether the hold was full or not. That is the whole innovation and it sounds like nothing. Sailing half empty is expensive. The line did it anyway. every month in both directions in winter. What they were selling was not speed, it was certainty. The times were good, mind you. Eastbound crossings averaged about 23 days against a typical 30. Westbound about 40 against 45, but the timetable is the product. Say you are a Liverpool merchant. You now know a ship leaves New York on a set day. You know, a reply can be in your hand by a date you can write down. By 1822, the line was running two sailings a month. Everyone else followed and they followed to New York because that is where the schedule was. Rival packet lines set up with New York as the western end of the route. That is how a port stops being one of several and becomes the default. Albian, who studied this harder than anyone, put the packets at the top of the list, ahead of the canal. That is worth sitting with for a moment, given what the ditch is about to do. The third decision is the famous one. Behind the American coast, there was a wall. The Appalachians run most of the length of the eastern United States. In 1800, there was no cheap way over them. Everything west of that ridge was on a different planet from the Atlantic. all that farmland, all that timber, all that grain. Not because it could not be moved, because of what moving it cost. Take a ton of freight at Buffalo on Lake Erie. Hauling it to New York City by road cost about $100. $100 a ton on wheat. A wagon carried a fraction of a ton, and the farmer paid by the mile. So for most of what the interior grew, the journey cost more than the crop was worth. You did not sell it east. You could not. You ate it. You fed it to a pig or you turned it into whiskey. Whiskey was the only way to make a wagon load worth the trip. That is the real map of early America. A coastline with money on it. An interior that could grow anything and sell almost none of it. The idea was obvious and nobody could do it. Water goes over walls that roads cannot. The Hudson already reaches the sea at Manhattan. Cut a channel west from it across the state to Lake Erie. Do that and you have joined the Atlantic Ocean to the Great Lakes. A farmer 800 m inland is suddenly on the coast. Very good idea. In 1809, an insane one. The United States had almost no canals, no engineering schools, and nobody alive who had built anything like it. New York sent people to Washington to ask the federal government to pay. Thomas Jefferson's answer is on the record. He called it little short of madness, a canal of 350 mi through the wilderness. He was not being unreasonable. He was right about American engineering in 1809. He was wrong about what New York would do anyway. Washington said no. The state built it alone. The push came from Dwit Clinton. He put his career behind it and had it hung around his neck for years. The nickname was Clinton's ditch. When people wanted to be unkind, and they often did, it was Clinton's folly. One state, no federal money, no president. Digging started on the 4th of July 1817 at Rome, New York. The numbers on the finished thing are worth hearing slowly. 363 mi long, 40 ft wide, 4 ft deep, 83 lift blocks. Because the land is not flat between the Hudson and Lake Erie, the canal climbs about 600 ft. Every foot of that is handled by a wooden gate and a chamber of water. $7 million carried by one state and it was built by men who were not engineers because there were no engineers. The people who surveyed and dug the eerie canal learned canal building by digging it. Afterwards, some of them built most of the other canals in the country. There was nowhere else the knowledge existed. Eight years of it, trees, rock, swamp, and a stretch through the Montazum marshes that made men sick in numbers. It opened on the 26th of October, 1825. Now, the number that redraws the map. Moving a ton from Buffalo to New York City had cost about $100. After the canal, it cost under 10. Roughly 90% gone. Not shaved, gone. The journey from the Hudson to Lake Erie had been a matter of weeks. It came down to about 5 days. Think about what that does to a farm in Ohio. Nothing about the farm changed. Same soil, same wheat, same family. The price of reaching a buyer fell by 90%. Every acre is now worth something it was not worth the year before. So, the canal did not move goods. It moved the coastline. It picked up the Atlantic edge of the United States and dragged it 800 miles inland. The point where all of it came back out to sea was one island. The state got its 7 million back in 9 years out of tolls. That is a remarkable public work by any standard. It is also the small prize. Grain came east, then timber, then everything else. And the boat that has gone one way has to come back. So the canal filled up going west as well. It carried people, settlers, tools, furniture, and the whole idea that the middle of America was somewhere you could get to. New York was not a port anymore. It was the mouth of a funnel with half a continent behind it. There is a second cargo on those packet ships, and it is easy to miss. Going east, the holds are full. cotton, timber, wheat, ash. Going west, they are close to empty. Manufactured goods are dense and valuable, so they do not fill a hole. A ship crossing back to New York had space and nothing to put in it. So, they sold the space to people. Steerage was the return load. It was cheap because the alternative was carrying nothing. A birth that earns anything beats ballast. That is why the immigrant trade concentrated on the New York run instead of spreading evenly across American ports. The ships were already going there on a schedule with room. And once people arrive, more arrive. The letters home named the ports the family already used. By 1855, the numbers were big enough that the state built somewhere to put them. Castle Garden opened as an immigrant depot on the 1st of August that year. It was the first station of its kind in America. Between 1855 and 1890, more than 8 million people came through it. 8 million, one building, one city before Ellis Island existed. Look at what that does to the machine. The labor to unload the warps arrives on the ships it is unloading. The workers for the workshops come the same way. So do the customers for the shops. Nobody planned that. It falls out of a timetable and an empty hold. The fourth decision is the one almost nobody knows about and Albian rated it enormously. New York went and took the South's cotton trade. Cotton that never needed to touch New York at all. From the 1820s, New York merchants built a triangle. Cotton goes from southern ports to Liverpool and La Havra. European manufactured goods come back to New York. Then coastal packets carry those goods south to the people who grew the cotton. Look at what that does. New York is not on the direct route. Charleston to Liverpool does not pass Manhattan. New York inserted itself anyway. It could do it because it already had the two other things. It had the scheduled ships crossing the Atlantic. It had the auction rooms and the credit that turned a cargo into cash. So a southern planter got a better price faster going the long way round through New York merchants than dealing direct. The men doing this became some of the richest in America. Anson Phelps is the name usually given and the money on that triangle is not the cotton. It is the commission, the freight, the insurance and the credit taken at every corner. New York is charging a toll on a journey it is not physically part of. That is the clearest single sentence about what this city became. The obvious question is why the south did not just do this itself. The answer is that shipping is not one business. It is four. You need vessels on a schedule. You need a market that can absorb a cargo in a day. You need credit against goods that have not sold yet. And you need insurance a stranger will accept. New York had assembled all four by the 1820s. A southern port could build ships. Building the other three takes decades. And by then, the habit has set. Everybody could see what was happening. Nobody could copy it. Pennsylvania went first and hardest. Philadelphia had been the largest city in America not long before. Now it was watching the country's trade route sail past up the Hudson. So the state built the main line of public works. Work started on the 4th of July 1826, one year after the Eerie opened. 395 miles of canal and railway stitched together at a cost of more than $12 million, nearly double what New York had spent. The reason it cost that is the Alagany Mountains. They do not have a convenient gap in them the way New York does. So, Pennsylvania went over the top. The Alagany Portridge Railroad was 36 mi of 10 inclined planes. Stationary steam engines and cables hauled the cars up the slopes. Mules pulled them along the flat parts. There were tunnels where neither would work. Canal boats were built in sections. A boat came out of the water, went over a mountain range, and went back in on the other side. and it worked, which is the genuinely impressive part. The trip across Pennsylvania fell from about 23 days to about 4. It still lost. It lost because New York's route was straight and flat, and Pennsylvania's was neither. Every incline is a delay, a cost. And one more thing that breaks. Pennsylvania's own account of it is blunt. It never restored Philadelphia's position. It could not match the cost or the ease of the eerie route. The state carried the depth and sold the whole line to the Pennsylvania Railroad in 1857. Baltimore tried the other answer. Instead of digging, it built a railway. The Baltimore and Ohio was chartered in 1827 and construction started the following year. Nobody in America had built a railroad on that scale. It was the right technology. It still did not take the trade back. By the time it reached the interior, everything else had moved. The merchants, the credit, the insurers, the shipping. That is the part that gets missed out about all four decisions. The advantage was physical for about 15 years. After that was made of habits, contracts, and relationships. There is no engineer answer to those. You cannot dig your way into somebody else's address book. So, Wall Street, there had been brokers on Wall Street since 1792. A couple dozen of them signed an agreement under a tree. It set out how they would trade with each other. That is 33 years before the canal opened. So, the story is not that Wall Street did not exist. The story is that it was not important yet and it was not where the country's money lived. That was Philadelphia, which had the Bank of the United States. the closest thing America had to a central bank and with it the gravity of being where the federal money sits. Three things moved it. The first is the cargo. Money follows goods because goods need financing before they move and settling after they arrive. By 1860, more than 80% of the nation's textiles came into America through New York. Not most. 80% of a whole country's cloth landing in one city. When that much lands on your wars, the lending happens on your street. So does the insuring and the discounting of bills. Nobody decides it. It is just the shortest distance. The second is the canal depth itself. The state had created something America barely had. a large, safe, tradable bond backed by a public asset that was visibly working. It pulled in capital from Europe. Investors who had never thought about America owned a piece of a ditch in upstate New York. The market they bought it through was in Manhattan. The third is politics. Through the 1830s, Andrew Jackson went to war with the Bank of the United States and its president, Nicholas Bidd. After Jackson was reelected in 1832, federal deposits were pulled out of the bank. They went into state banks instead, and a lot of those were in New York. The bank's charter ran out in 1836. An attempt to revive it as a Pennsylvania bank failed in 1841. Philadelphia lost the institution. New York already had the trade and now it had the deposits, too. That is the order of events. the harbor, the auctions, the packets, the canal, the cotton, then the money. Wall Street did not choose New York. The cargo chose New York and Wall Street went where the cargo was. One more decision and it is 14 years before the canal opened. In 1811, a state commission published a plan for Manhattan north of the builtup part. It drew the whole island as a grid, numbered streets across, numbered avenues up, identical rectangular blocks over farmland and rock and marsh where almost nobody lived. There is no beauty in it, and that was not an accident. The commissioners argued it in plain terms. People live in right angled houses, and the plain rectangle is cheap to build on and easy to buy and sell. That last part is the important part. The grid turned an island into inventory. A piece of Manhattan became a standard unit. It could be described in a sentence. Sold to a stranger, borrowed against, speculated on decades before anyone lived there. So when the trade arrived and the people followed, the city was not improvising. The lots existed, the map was drawn. New York had put its land into a form that money could move through. Then the money showed up. The population figures do the rest of the talking. In 1820, the city had about 123,000 people. By 1860, it had 813,000, roughly 7 times bigger in 40 years. That is not a growth rate. That is a place being filled up by something. It is worth saying what this costs at the other end. Buffalo, Rochester, Santa Cruz, Rome, Utica, Albany. That is the list I promised you. The towns along the route boomed. Buffalo boomed hardest because Buffalo was the hinge. It was the point where the lake traffic became canal traffic and everything had to be handled. Grain, then milling, then everything that follows. A lot of money arriving in a small place. Then the railways came and the traffic changed again and again. The boats that built those towns stopped needing them. The canal is still there and most of it is a recreational waterway now. There are cyclists on the toe path where the mules used to walk. Some of you are living on top of one of the most important pieces of infrastructure in American history. It is a footpath. A working canal became a piece. A working canal became a nice place to spend a Sunday. That is what happens to infrastructure that gets overtaken. New York kept the advantage because New York was the end of the funnel. not a point along it. Being the place where everything comes out is a different job from being a place pass through. It survives the traffic changing. The towns did not have that. I'm not going to tie this up neatly because there is one sentence that does it. New York is not a financial city that happens to have a harbor. It is a harbor that got handed a continent and the finance grew on top of that like moss. Four decisions inside eight years. An auction law in 1817. A timetable in 1818. A ditch begun in 1817 and finished in 1825. A triangle through the cotton ports in the 20s. Every one of them is a way of removing uncertainty from somebody else's business and charging for it. That is still the business. The exchange, the towers, the clearing houses, the insurers. Different century, same trade. The city is the receipt, right? The canal towns. Go and answer that question if you skipped it earlier. That half of the comment section will be better than this video. If you are one of them, I would rather have your version than another book. The one to watch next is how Singapore got rich. Same shape, other side of the world. Another place with nothing but a harbor that had to decide what to be. That's one and the rest of them are in the how the countries got rich playlist.
